items.title: CEO of $21 billion Cerebras says it’s minted 1,000 employees into millionaires—but warns that drastic changes in fortunes can be ‘really stressful’
items.summary:
Employees at some of the largest tech companies are scoring big thanks to stock purchase benefits . Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman says he’s proud that his $21.7 billion AI company has turned over a thousand of its staffers into millionaires. But he knows firsthand how quickly those fortunes can change—and says employees shouldn’t get too caught up in watching their net worths yo-yo.

“What we’ve done with our team first, we made more than a thousand millionaires,” Feldman recently said on the Sourcery with Molly O’Shea channel. “That’s something I’m really proud of. I think that’s our job as leaders, to make our guys wealthy. We talked about the fact that we’re not in this for the short run, that the daily fluctuations are not what they should watch.”

As tech companies rule the U.S. stock market, all it takes is a bad earnings report or a shift in investor sentiment to send company shares on a rollercoaster ride. 

Now, founders and employees alike can watch their fortunes fluctuate in the span of one day. Eligible employees at Cerebras can buy company stock directly through deductions from their paychecks at a potential 15% discount, according to the company’s 2026 Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP). In May of this year, Cerebras had a standout IPO offering 30 million Class A shares at price of $185.00 per share, raising $5.55 billion.

Feldman’s share was estimated to be worth about $3.2 billion following the IPO, but the CEO warned workers against watching their wealth swing at the whim of the stock market.

items.title: Elon Musk says Tesla self-driving makes seniors safer. Tesla’s own fine print says the 93-year-old in its ad must watch the road
items.summary:
In July, Tesla posted a video of a 93-year-old San Diego resident named Lois using a red Tesla equipped with Full Self-Driving (FSD) Supervised software to make road trips to see her family and run errands. 

“I don’t have to wait for someone, and it’s been a wonderful experience,” Lois said to the camera after a video montage of her visiting her grandkids and smiling at the beach.

Tesla has promoted FSD Supervised, which can change lanes and make turns, as a way for seniors to keep their independence. The company is now rolling out a new version of the software. Reposting another video in March of an 87-year-old woman testing out an FSD-equipped Cybertruck, the company said “FSD Supervised can give you back your freedom.” Elon Musk has also said that Tesla self-driving “enables safer mobility for senior citizens” on X . 

But Tesla’s promise comes with a catch: FSD Supervised still requires a driver to monitor the road. Tesla added “Supervised” to the name after California regulators accused it of misleading customers about what the software could do. That raises a safety dilemma for older drivers who are turning to FSD Supervised as their driving abilities decline. Tesla itself has cautioned that none of FSD Supervised’s features can replace an attentive person at the wheel, which is why some legal experts question marketing it to older drivers. Lawyers say the pitch could expose Tesla, too: a federal jury has already found the company partly liable for a fatal crash involving Autopilot, its more basic driver-assistance system.

“A technology that requires a capable…
items.t: Elon Musk says Tesla self-driving makes seniors safer. Tesla’s own fine print says the 93-year-old in its ad must watch the road

items.title: Billionaire Fanatics CEO opened his first business at 12, and nearly lost it all by 16: ‘I went from death… to making $10-15 million a year as a kid’
items.summary:
Fanatics has become a one-stop shop for sports fans looking to rep their favorite teams and athletes. But the company has grown into a powerhouse in its own right, striking partnerships with nearly every major U.S. sports league, including the NFL, NBA, and MLB, and generating roughly $14 billion in annual revenue.

For cofounder and CEO Michael Rubin , however, the road to building that empire nearly ended before he turned 20.

Rubin caught the entrepreneurial bug at just 12 years old, when most kids are more concerned with middle school homework than starting a business. By 13, he was selling ski equipment out of his parents’ basement in Pennsylvania, and a year later, he had opened his own storefront just down the road from his home. He was making money quickly—and even went in with his friend in buying a Porchse before he could even legally drive.

But in around 1988, there was an unusually warm winter, and so his customers weren’t coming.

“It didn’t snow that year,” Rubin recalled in a recent conversation with podcaster David Senra . “End of the year, I had $200,000 of bills, $80,000 of inventory, and I was sitting right in front of bankruptcy.”

To get himself out of the hole, he negotiated his debts down to $35,000, went door to door borrowing money from neighbors, and used the proceeds from a new venture in the closeout business to repay his loan within three weeks. Five years later, at 21, Rubin was generating $150 million in sales buying and selling closeout merchandise.

“I went from death in its eyes, bankrupt, thought I was complete failure, giving up on…
items.t: Billionaire Fanatics CEO opened his first business at 12, and nearly lost it all by 16: ‘I went from death… to making $10-15 million a year as a kid’

items.title: OpenAI asked me to assess GPT-2 before its release. The stakes are even higher now
items.summary:
In 2019, I was at an artificial intelligence workshop at a D.C. think tank when OpenAI gave a presentation about a new language model they were developing called GPT-2. The presentation was intended as a show-and-tell, but I I started thinking beyond the technology to its potential implications for political influence and national security. 

I followed up with OpenAI and raised the potential, following on the heels of the 2016 foreign election interference, that the technology could be used by nefarious actors for large-scale misinformation campaigns. OpenAI brought me on as an early academic collaborator to study whether a machine could write political content enough to fool the people it was aimed at, such as leaders or the public.

In retrospect, I was primed to see those risks because I had encountered a similar dynamic in my military career. As an Air Force officer, I had seen how emerging technologies could take on lives of their own. The Predator drone had gone from a surveillance platform to an armed aircraft that became a hammer for the U.S. military that made everything look like a nail. Obama said in reference to armed drones that it was “so easy to use them without thinking through all the ramifications.”

I wondered whether AI-generated content might follow a similar trajectory, developed as a research experiment in advancing artificial intelligence’s ability to understand and generate human language, but ultimately being captured for misuses, perhaps political manipulation or misinformation at scale.

Working with a colleague at OpenAI and another who would…
items.t: OpenAI asked me to assess GPT-2 before its release. The stakes are even higher now

items.title: Medicaid kids with autism are diagnosed at 5, then wait 201 more days for help
items.summary:
A mother leaves her pediatrician’s office with a referral and a warning that acting early matters. Now she has to find a specialist who accepts her insurance and is accepting patients. Make the calls. Complete the forms. Wait.

Months later, often years, her child receives an autism diagnosis. Then someone hands her another list of people to call.

We call parents who navigate this process tireless advocates. The compliment conceals an institutional failure. Autism care depends on families doing the unpaid work of making disconnected institutions function as a system. Parents pay with their time, income and exhaustion. Children pay in time without appropriate support.

Among children covered by Medicaid, the average age at autism diagnosis is five, and the average delay between diagnosis and treatment is 201 days.

When Dennis helped develop Diggy, which Esther supports as a founding advisor to its investor, Treehub, the goal was to address a persistent gap in autism care. Families often wait months for answers, while their children could benefit from support today. Diggy was designed to help parents take meaningful steps earlier, offering personalized guidance and activities that can begin before a formal diagnosis and support a family through a diagnosis.

Families can begin using Diggy the week they sign up, without having to wait for a formal diagnosis. Of the roughly 20,000 children who have used the platform, 60% started before age four and 75% before age six, with the average starting age just three. items.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ opens to $120 million despite GTA VI—and its audience explains why
items.summary:
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to an estimated $120 million in North America this weekend, nearly three times the $44 million debut of its 2023 predecessor, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes . The Lionsgate prequel added $105 million overseas for a $225 million global launch, returning the franchise to the three-figure heights of its original run.

It did so in the shadow of Grand Theft Auto VI , the long-awaited Rockstar Games release that arrived one day earlier. Fans and industry insiders alike speculated that the game, which topped $1 billion in pre-sales ahead of its Nov. 19 launch, would monopolize the attention economy and drain an already thin November box office .

In hindsight, releasing a Hunger Games movie the day after GTA VI may have been a clever piece of counterprogramming. “I think the marketplace has already spoken,” Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian told the Associated Press. 

Two franchises, two very different audiences 

Both GTA and The Hunger Games are now multigenerational action franchises, but the former has always targeted men, mostly young-adult to 40-year-old gamers drawn to its edgy depictions of criminal violence. The Hunger Games , meanwhile, has its roots in teen readers and women.

Like the five films before it, Sunrise on the Reaping is adapted from Suzanne Collins’s young-adult novels. It centers on 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, played by Joseph Zada, but the series was built around its heroine, Katniss Everdeen. Jennifer Lawrence, who led the original four films as Katniss, returns for a brief epilogue cameo.

items.title: Why is gas suddenly cheaper? Five factors driving the drop to $3.64 a gallon
items.summary:
The average price of gasoline in the U.S. has plunged nearly 90 cents a gallon in two months, down to its lowest level since the early days of the Iran war, coming just in time for Thanksgiving travel.

Context, of course, matters. The average price for a gallon of regular unleaded was $3.64 on Monday. Though that’s 57 cents higher than the price a year ago, according to AAA, it has come down precipitously of late. And it would only have to fall a bit further to $3.58 to hit where it stood on Thanksgiving Day 2022. Over the weekend, in some parts of the country, prices at the pump could be seen hovering at—or occasionally even below—the $3 mark, a huge psychological break for consumers who have suffered through years of rising prices.

“The scale of decline has been a little bit surprising,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “But given how things have developed, it’s not really a shock.”

So why have prices fallen so sharply since late September? It’s a combination of geopolitical factors in the Middle East, typical seasonal declines, and refinery operational issues. And, no, there wasn’t any conspiracy to keep prices higher ahead of the midterm elections. However, President Donald Trump’s actions are key contributors.

Here are the five main factors causing fuel prices—especially gasoline—to tumble:

More oil exports are exiting the Middle East, including from the now-infamous Strait of Hormuz

items.t: Why is gas suddenly cheaper? Five factors driving the drop to $3.64 a gallon

items.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
items.summary:
Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes?

In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north.

That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way.

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Trump’s ‘assurance’ to Nvidia’s board over national security may have just provided it with protection from a major source of legal danger

A White House spokesperson confirmed Trump’s role to Fortune : “President Trump was totally involved, and this is a great decision by the Nvidia board. We have to protect our geniuses.” 

Huang, who cofounded the semiconductor chip giant 33 years ago, resigned earlier this month following revelations of an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence reportedly deemed a Chinese operative. Alice Huang was also an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, which is being investigated for allegedly smuggling at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips . The Nvidia CEO also faces allegations of affairs with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, and a second unnamed Nvidia employee; it is unclear which scandal prompted his resignation.

Nvidia’s board reportedly met on Sunday night, just hours after Trump made a call on social media for Huang’s reinstatement .

items.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
items.summary:
On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing

During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.

Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels.

items.t: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial

One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.

The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.

items.title: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears
items.summary:
Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves

European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills.

The Dutch month-ahead contract – the European benchmark for gas prices over the next four weeks – rose by as much as 8.6% to €96.08, before settling up 4% at €92.50.

items.t: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears

items.title: Cost of renting in Britain to rise twice as fast as buying amid shortage of properties
items.summary:
Rents to rise by 14% until at least 2029, Hamptons predicts, as high demand for properties and low supply push up costs for tenants

The cost of renting a home in Britain is expected to rise about twice as fast as that of buying one until at least 2029, according to research, with shrinking supply pushing up the prices paid by tenants.

Rents on newly agreed lets are forecast to grow by 14.2% between 2026 and 2029, compared with house price growth of 7.2%, according to forecasts from estate agent Hamptons.

Continue reading...
items.t: Cost of renting in Britain to rise twice as fast as buying amid shortage of properties

items.title: UK taxpayers held more than £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows
items.summary:
Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama, raising fears over cost to public purse

The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures.

items.t: UK taxpayers held more that £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows

Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Golf did not move from outside her London home while she was on holiday in Canada, but a similar vehicle with a fraudulent copy of her registration racked up penalty notices totalling £2,560 across five London boroughs.

items.title: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout
items.summary:
New draft text released at Cop31 summit after countries fail to agree on electrification and finance for developing world

Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the global need to phase out fossil fuels.

The co-conveners of the Cop31 UN climate summit, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday until late evening as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress.

items.title: Inside the race to put computers in the human brain
items.summary:
A robotic arm drills a circle into the patient’s skull, then places a quarter-size device onto the brain tissue. Dangling from it are 64 wires, each thinner than a human hair. Electrodes along the wires pick up electrical signals from neurons in the brain, and the implant transmits that data to a phone or tablet. The patient can text friends, post on social media, and even play video games—all without lifting a finger.

That’s the promise of the N1 implant made by Neuralink, the brain-computer interface (BCI) company owned by Elon Musk. Neuralink has made science fiction a reality for the approximately 26 people using the device today in the product’s testing phase. All have severe disabilities, but Musk founded the company in 2016 with the goal of far broader adoption. In 2017 he argued that humans will need to connect our brains to technology to keep up with artificial intelligence and avoid “being left behind and being effectively useless, or like a pet.” By 2025, Neuralink was valued at roughly $9.7 billion.

Although no brain implants are on the U.S. market yet, the first one that becomes available will be a watershed moment—for the tech sector, for society, arguably for humanity—setting off what those in the industry expect to be a decades-long process to merge our minds with machines. BCIs stand to become increasingly interwoven in our everyday lives, spawning new businesses and demanding new norms to govern their use.

At stake for the companies pioneering these devices is a potentially massive market, both for the devices and the vast troves of data they’ll…
items.t: Inside the race to put computers in the human brain

items.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
items.summary:
Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

items.t: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
